## Introduction
In this homework, I will continue working with the Seoul Bike Sharing dataset from HW9. I will use the tidymodels package to fit different models and compare how well they predict daily bike rentals.

## Part 1: Reading the Data

### Loading Packages

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(tidymodels)
```

### Reading the Dataset

The dataset contains hourly bike rentals and weather information from Seoul.

```{r}
bike_data <- read_csv(
  "https://www4.stat.ncsu.edu/~online/datasets/SeoulBikeData.csv",
  locale = locale(encoding = "Latin1")
)

head(bike_data)
dim(bike_data)
```

The dataset has 8,760 rows and 14 columns.

## Part 2: Exploratory Data Analysis

### Checking Missing Values

First, I checked whether the dataset contains any missing values.

```{r}
colSums(is.na(bike_data))
```

There are no missing values in the dataset.

### Checking Column Types

I checked the data types and summary statistics to understand the variables.

```{r}
str(bike_data)

bike_data |>
  select(where(is.numeric)) |>
  summary()
```

### Checking Categorical Variables

I checked the values in the categorical columns.

```{r}
unique(bike_data$Seasons)
unique(bike_data$Holiday)
unique(bike_data$`Functioning Day`)
```

### Converting Date

The Date column was stored as text, so I converted it into a date format.

```{r}
bike_data <- bike_data |>
  mutate(Date = dmy(Date))

head(bike_data$Date)
```

### Converting Categorical Variables

I converted the categorical variables into factors.

```{r}
bike_data <- bike_data |>
  mutate(
    Seasons = as.factor(Seasons),
    Holiday = as.factor(Holiday),
    `Functioning Day` = as.factor(`Functioning Day`)
  )
```

### Renaming Columns

I renamed the variables using lower snake case to make them easier to use.

```{r}
bike_data <- bike_data |>
  rename_with(~ "date", .cols = Date) |>
  rename_with(~ "bike_count", .cols = `Rented Bike Count`) |>
  rename_with(~ "hour", .cols = Hour) |>
  rename_with(~ "temp", .cols = starts_with("Temperature")) |>
  rename_with(~ "humidity", .cols = starts_with("Humidity")) |>
  rename_with(~ "wind_speed", .cols = starts_with("Wind speed")) |>
  rename_with(~ "visibility", .cols = starts_with("Visibility")) |>
  rename_with(~ "dew_point_temp", .cols = starts_with("Dew point")) |>
  rename_with(~ "solar_radiation", .cols = starts_with("Solar Radiation")) |>
  rename_with(~ "rainfall", .cols = starts_with("Rainfall")) |>
  rename_with(~ "snowfall", .cols = starts_with("Snowfall")) |>
  rename_with(~ "seasons", .cols = Seasons) |>
  rename_with(~ "holiday", .cols = Holiday) |>
  rename_with(~ "functioning_day", .cols = `Functioning Day`)

names(bike_data)
```

### Summary Statistics

I calculated the mean, median, minimum and maximum number of bike rentals.

```{r}
bike_data |>
  summarize(
    mean_bikes = mean(bike_count),
    median_bikes = median(bike_count),
    min_bikes = min(bike_count),
    max_bikes = max(bike_count)
  )
```

### Removing Non-Functioning Hours

I removed the observations when the bike rental system was not operating.

```{r}
bike_data <- bike_data |>
  filter(functioning_day == "Yes") |>
  select(-functioning_day)

dim(bike_data)
```

### Creating Daily Data

I combined hourly observations into daily observations. I used the sum for bike rentals, rainfall and snowfall and the mean for the other weather variables.

```{r}
bike_daily <- bike_data |>
  group_by(date, seasons, holiday) |>
  summarize(
    bike_count = sum(bike_count),
    rainfall = sum(rainfall),
    snowfall = sum(snowfall),
    temp = mean(temp),
    humidity = mean(humidity),
    wind_speed = mean(wind_speed),
    visibility = mean(visibility),
    dew_point_temp = mean(dew_point_temp),
    solar_radiation = mean(solar_radiation),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

head(bike_daily)
dim(bike_daily)
```

The daily dataset has 353 rows and 12 columns.

## Part 3: Splitting the Data

I split the daily dataset into training and testing sets. I used 75% of the data for training and 25% for testing. I also used seasons to keep the seasonal distribution similar in both sets.

```{r}
set.seed(558)

bike_split <- initial_split(
  bike_daily,
  prop = 0.75,
  strata = seasons
)

bike_train <- training(bike_split)
bike_test <- testing(bike_split)

dim(bike_train)
dim(bike_test)
```

### Creating 10-Fold Cross-Validation

I created 10 folds using the training data. These folds will be used to compare the models before testing them on the test data.

```{r}
set.seed(558)

bike_folds <- vfold_cv(
  bike_train,
  v = 10
)

bike_folds
```

## Part 4: Fitting Multiple Linear Regression Models

### Recipe 1: Basic Model

For the first model, I created a recipe to prepare the data for linear regression. I used the date to create a weekday or weekend variable and removed the date from the predictors. I also standardized the numeric predictors and created dummy variables for the categorical variables.

```{r}
recipe1 <- recipe(bike_count ~ ., data = bike_train) |>
  step_date(date, features = "dow") |>
  step_mutate(
    day_type = factor(
      if_else(date_dow %in% c("Sat", "Sun"),
              "Weekend", "Weekday")
    )
  ) |>
  step_rm(date, date_dow) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

recipe1
```


### Recipe 2: Adding Interaction Terms

For the second recipe, I used the same preprocessing steps as Recipe 1 and added interactions between seasons and holiday, seasons and temperature and temperature and rainfall.

```{r}
recipe2 <- recipe(bike_count ~ ., data = bike_train) |>
  step_date(date, features = "dow") |>
  step_mutate(
    day_type = factor(
      if_else(date_dow %in% c("Sat", "Sun"),
              "Weekend", "Weekday")
    )
  ) |>
  step_rm(date, date_dow) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
 step_interact(
  terms = ~ starts_with("seasons_"):starts_with("holiday_") +
    starts_with("seasons_"):temp +
    temp:rainfall
)

recipe2
```

### Recipe 3: Adding Quadratic Terms

For the third recipe, I kept the interactions from Recipe 2 and added squared terms for standardized temperature and humidity. This allows the model to capture possible curved relationships with bike rentals.

```{r}
recipe3 <- recipe(bike_count ~ ., data = bike_train) |>
  step_date(date, features = "dow") |>
  step_mutate(
    day_type = factor(
      if_else(date_dow %in% c("Sat", "Sun"),
              "Weekend", "Weekday")
    )
  ) |>
  step_rm(date, date_dow) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
step_interact(
  terms = ~ starts_with("seasons_"):starts_with("holiday_") +
    starts_with("seasons_"):temp +
    temp:rainfall
) |>
step_mutate(
  temp_squared = temp^2,
  humidity_squared = humidity^2
)

recipe3

```

### Setting Up the Linear Regression Model

I used linear regression with the lm engine to fit all three recipes.

```{r}
lm_model <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm")

lm_model
```

### Creating Workflows

I created a separate workflow for each recipe using the same linear regression model.

```{r}
workflow1 <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(recipe1) |>
  add_model(lm_model)

workflow2 <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(recipe2) |>
  add_model(lm_model)

workflow3 <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(recipe3) |>
  add_model(lm_model)
```

### Fitting Models Using 10-Fold Cross-Validation

I used the 10 folds created earlier to evaluate the three models. I used RMSE to compare their prediction errors.

```{r}
set.seed(558)

lm_cv1 <- fit_resamples(
  workflow1,
  resamples = bike_folds,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse, mae)
)

lm_cv2 <- fit_resamples(
  workflow2,
  resamples = bike_folds,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse, mae)
)

lm_cv3 <- fit_resamples(
  workflow3,
  resamples = bike_folds,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse, mae)
)

```

### Checking Cross-Validation Warnings

Models 2 and 3 produced a rank-deficiency warning in Fold06 during cross-validation. This may be related to the interaction terms and limited variation in that fold. The models still produced cross-validation results, so I continued comparing them using RMSE and MAE.

### Comparing the Three Models

I collected the cross-validation results and compared the average RMSE and MAE for each model.

```{r}
lm_results <- bind_rows(
  collect_metrics(lm_cv1) |> mutate(model = "Model 1"),
  collect_metrics(lm_cv2) |> mutate(model = "Model 2"),
  collect_metrics(lm_cv3) |> mutate(model = "Model 3")
)

lm_results |>
  select(model, .metric, mean, std_err)
```

### Selecting the Best Linear Regression Model

I selected the model with the lowest average cross-validation RMSE.

```{r}
best_lm <- lm_results |>
  filter(.metric == "rmse") |>
  arrange(mean) |>
  slice(1)

best_lm
```

### Fitting the Selected Model

I used the selected recipe and fitted the model using the full training portion of the original split.

```{r}
best_workflow <- switch(
  best_lm$model[[1]],
  "Model 1" = workflow1,
  "Model 2" = workflow2,
  "Model 3" = workflow3
)

final_lm <- last_fit(
  best_workflow,
  split = bike_split,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse, mae)
)

collect_metrics(final_lm)
```

### Final Linear Regression Coefficients

I extracted the fitted linear regression model and displayed its coefficients.

```{r}
final_lm_fit <- extract_workflow(final_lm) |>
  extract_fit_parsnip()

tidy(final_lm_fit)
```

### Linear Regression Results

Among the three linear regression models, Model 3 had the lowest cross-validation RMSE of approximately 3,046. This model included interaction terms and quadratic terms for temperature and humidity.

When I evaluated Model 3 on the test data, the RMSE was approximately 3,059 and the MAE was 2,132. These results suggest that adding interactions and quadratic terms improved prediction accuracy compared with the basic linear regression model.

## Part 5: Regression Tree

In this section, I will fit a regression tree to predict daily bike rentals. A regression tree splits the data into smaller groups based on predictor values.

### Creating the Regression Tree Recipe

I created a recipe to prepare the data for the regression tree. I used the date to create a weekday or weekend variable and removed the original date column.

```{r}
tree_recipe <- recipe(bike_count ~ ., data = bike_train) |>
  step_date(date, features = "dow") |>
  step_mutate(
    day_type = factor(
      if_else(date_dow %in% c("Sat", "Sun"),
              "Weekend", "Weekday")
    )
  ) |>
  step_rm(date, date_dow)

tree_recipe
```

### Setting Up the Regression Tree Model

I used the rpart engine to fit a regression tree. I will tune the cost complexity, tree depth, and minimum number of observations in a node to find a model with lower prediction error.

```{r}
tree_model <- decision_tree(
  cost_complexity = tune(),
  tree_depth = tune(),
  min_n = tune()
) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("regression")

tree_model
```

### Creating the Regression Tree Workflow

I combined the regression tree recipe and model into a workflow.

```{r}
tree_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(tree_recipe) |>
  add_model(tree_model)

tree_workflow
```

### Creating the Tuning Grid

I created a grid of values for cost complexity, tree depth, and minimum node size. I will compare these combinations using cross-validation to find the best regression tree.

```{r}
tree_grid <- grid_regular(
  cost_complexity(),
  tree_depth(),
  min_n(),
  levels = 3
)

tree_grid
```

### Tuning the Regression Tree

I used 10-fold cross-validation to compare the different regression tree settings. I used RMSE and MAE to measure prediction error.

```{r}
set.seed(558)

tree_tuned <- tune_grid(
  tree_workflow,
  resamples = bike_folds,
  grid = tree_grid,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse, mae)
)

collect_metrics(tree_tuned)
```

### Selecting the Best Regression Tree

I selected the regression tree settings with the lowest average cross-validation RMSE.

```{r}
best_tree <- select_best(
  tree_tuned,
  metric = "rmse"
)

best_tree
```

### Fitting the Final Regression Tree

I used the best tuning parameters to finalize the regression tree workflow. I then fitted the model on the training data and evaluated its predictions on the test data.

```{r}
final_tree_workflow <- finalize_workflow(
  tree_workflow,
  best_tree
)

final_tree <- last_fit(
  final_tree_workflow,
  split = bike_split,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse, mae)
)

collect_metrics(final_tree)
```

### Comparing the Final Models

I compared the test RMSE and MAE of the best linear regression model and the regression tree.

```{r}
model_comparison <- bind_rows(
  collect_metrics(final_lm) |>
    mutate(model = "Linear Regression"),
  collect_metrics(final_tree) |>
    mutate(model = "Regression Tree")
)

model_comparison |>
  select(model, .metric, .estimate)
```

## Conclusion

In this homework, I used the Seoul Bike Sharing dataset to compare multiple linear regression models and a regression tree for predicting daily bike rentals.

Among the linear regression models, Model 3 performed the best. It included interaction terms and quadratic terms for temperature and humidity.

The final linear regression model had a test RMSE of approximately 3,059 and MAE of 2,132. The regression tree had a higher RMSE of 3,814 and MAE of 2,866.

Overall, the linear regression model performed better on the test data. This suggests that the interaction and quadratic terms helped capture the relationships in this dataset better than the regression tree.
